evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Architectural modularity in AI systems with strict separation and no cross-modal feedback a greater reduction in system accuracy for ambiguous perceptual inputs than for unambiguous inputs, relative to integrated architectures]

[PATH:empirical] Controlled experiment comparing modular (e.g., separate vision and language modules) vs. integrated (e.g., multimodal transformer) architectures on tasks with systematically varied input ambiguity (e.g., blurred images, noisy text) and measuring accuracy drop per ambiguity level — Directly tests the hypothesis by manipulating the key variable (architectural modularity vs. integration) and the independent variable (input ambiguity), providing causal evidence on accuracy reduction.

[PATH:literature] Literature review and meta-analysis of published benchmarks (e.g., on VQA, audio-visual speech recognition) that compare modular and integrated systems, focusing on performance under ambiguous inputs — Synthesizes existing evidence across multiple studies to assess whether the hypothesized pattern holds generally, increasing statistical power and generalizability over a single experiment.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical analysis using information theory or Bayesian inference to model how strict separation without cross-modal feedback amplifies errors under ambiguity due to loss of mutual information between modalities — Provides a formal causal mechanism explaining why modularity would cause greater accuracy reduction under ambiguity, which can be used to generate testable predictions and refine the hypothesis.

scope.domain: modular vs. integrated architectures under varying input ambiguity levels

[PATH:empirical] Controlled experiments comparing modular vs. monolithic deep learning architectures on ambiguous image classification tasks (e.g., ImageNet-C or CIFAR-10-C with adversarial perturbations) — Directly tests whether modularity improves robustness and adaptability under perceptual ambiguity, providing quantitative metrics (e.g., accuracy drop, recovery time) to confirm or refute the hypothesis.

[PATH:literature] Systematic review of published studies on modular neural networks and their performance on out-of-distribution or noisy inputs (e.g., from NeurIPS, ICML, or ICLR proceedings 2020-2024) — Synthesizes existing evidence across the global AI research community to assess whether the claimed enhancement is consistently observed or disputed, clarifying the status of the hypothesis.

C007.subject: Loss of feedback pathways specifically in the ventral visual stream
C007.object: reduced accuracy during ambiguous perceptual input processing
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Loss of feedback pathways specifically in the ventral visual stream reduced accuracy during ambiguous perceptual input processing]

[PATH:empirical] Lesion studies in non-human primates selectively disrupting feedback connections from V2/V4 to V1 while preserving feedforward pathways, followed by behavioral testing on ambiguous figure-ground perception tasks — Directly tests whether loss of ventral stream feedback alone causes accuracy deficits in ambiguous perception, controlling for competing modularity hypotheses via anatomical specificity.

[PATH:theoretical] Computational modeling of hierarchical predictive coding with and without ventral-stream feedback ablation, simulating ambiguous input processing and comparing accuracy outcomes to human psychophysical data — Provides mechanistic grounding for causal role of feedback, allowing isolation of shared latent space explanations and testing of qualifier conditions.

[PATH:literature] Systematic review and meta-analysis of human fMRI or MEG studies contrasting effective connectivity in ventral stream during ambiguous vs. unambiguous perception, with statistical control for dorsal stream involvement — Evaluates existing evidence for specificity of ventral feedback in ambiguity resolution, identifying gaps and converging support for the hypothesis.

qualifier.condition: when top-down contextual priors are disconnected from bottom-up inference and the competing modularity hypothesis is controlled for
qualifier.uncertainty: shared latent space explanation is ruled out by lesion-specific behavioral dissociations

C008.subject: Integration of feedforward and feedback processes
C008.predicate: is more crucial than loss of feedback pathways for
C008.object: maintaining accuracy during ambiguous perceptual input processing
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Integration of feedforward and feedback processes maintaining accuracy during ambiguous perceptual input processing]

[PATH:empirical] Dynamic causal modeling (DCM) of fMRI data during bistable perception tasks (e.g., Necker cube or Rubin vase) to compare effective connectivity of feedforward vs. feedback pathways in ambiguous vs. unambiguous conditions. — If feedforward-feedback integration is more crucial than loss of feedback alone, DCM should show that disruption of integration (e.g., via altered coupling) impairs accuracy more than selective attenuation of feedback connections during early perceptual processing.

[PATH:theoretical] Computational modeling of hierarchical neural networks with controlled feedforward-feedback integration and selective feedback ablation, simulating ambiguous input processing (e.g., with noise or occlusion) within the first 200 ms. — This approach can directly test the hypothesis by comparing accuracy under conditions of intact integration versus isolated feedback loss, providing mechanistic predictions for empirical validation.

[PATH:literature] Literature review of studies on visual perception in patients with disrupted feedback pathways (e.g., schizophrenia or stroke) versus those with impaired integration (e.g., autism spectrum disorders), focusing on ambiguous stimulus tasks. — Existing clinical and experimental data can be synthesized to assess whether integration deficits correlate more strongly with perceptual accuracy loss than feedback pathway damage alone, supporting or refuting the hypothesis.

scope.domain: feedback and feedforward integration in hierarchical perception

qualifier.temporal: during initial perceptual processing (within first 200 ms after stimulus onset)

C011.subject: Forced alignment of shared latent spaces via contrastive objectives
C011.object: top-down contextual priors constraining bottom-up perceptual inference
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Forced alignment of shared latent spaces via contrastive objectives top-down contextual priors constraining bottom-up perceptual inference]

[PATH:empirical] A controlled experiment comparing contrastive vs. non-contrastive alignment on paired cross-modal data (e.g., image-caption pairs) with matched latent dimensions, measuring the degree to which top-down contextual priors (e.g., language) influence bottom-up perceptual inference (e.g., visual feature reconstruction) under varying levels of modality-specific noise. — Directly tests the hypothesis by manipulating the alignment method and noise, providing causal evidence for or against restoration of top-down constraints.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical analysis of the geometry of contrastively aligned latent spaces, examining whether the contrastive objective inherently induces a structure that supports top-down modulation (e.g., via conditional independence or mutual information bounds) and identifying conditions under which feedback pathways are necessary. — Clarifies the mechanism behind the hypothesized restoration, addressing the uncertainty about robustness to noise and the need for explicit feedback.

[PATH:literature] Literature review of studies on representational alignment in multi-modal AI (e.g., CLIP, ALIGN, VLM benchmarks), focusing on experiments that test top-down effects on perception (e.g., language-guided visual attention or reconstruction) and whether contrastive objectives alone suffice or require additional architectural components like cross-attention. — Synthesizes existing evidence to assess the hypothesis's plausibility and identifies gaps or contradictory findings that could confirm or refute it.

qualifier.condition: when the contrastive loss is applied to paired cross-modal data and the latent dimensionality is matched
qualifier.uncertainty: it is unknown whether this restoration is robust to modality-specific noise or requires explicit feedback pathways

C012.subject: Presence of shared latent spaces
C012.object: top-down contextual priors to constrain bottom-up perceptual inference
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Presence of shared latent spaces top-down contextual priors to constrain bottom-up perceptual inference]

[PATH:empirical] Controlled experiments comparing performance of multi-modal AI systems (e.g., CLIP, GATO) on perceptual tasks with and without explicit shared latent space regularization, measuring top-down constraint effects on bottom-up inference accuracy. — Directly tests whether shared latent spaces causally enable top-down priors to constrain inference, by manipulating presence vs. absence of such spaces and measuring downstream perceptual outcomes.

[PATH:theoretical] Computational analysis of representational geometry in models trained with shared latent spaces (e.g., using CKA, RSA) to quantify alignment between modalities and correlate with effectiveness of top-down modulation during inference. — Provides mechanistic evidence: if shared latent spaces are the mechanism, then higher alignment should predict stronger top-down constraint, enabling confirmation or refutation of the hypothesized causal relationship.

[PATH:literature] Systematic literature review of recent (2020s) papers on multi-modal representational alignment, focusing on studies that report or fail to report top-down contextual effects in models with and without shared latent spaces. — Aggregates existing evidence across the global research community to assess whether the disputed hypothesis is consistently supported or contradicted, given the current theoretical discourse.
